title: A language and its written forms
paragraphs: In fifteenth-century Joseon, Korean was a spoken language with a rich social life, but the main prestige writing system used in state administration and elite scholarship was Classical Chinese. Koreans had also developed methods for representing Korean elements through adaptations of Chinese characters. These practices were important and sophisticated, yet they did not provide the kind of straightforward, broadly usable representation of Korean sounds later associated with Hangul.

The difficulty was not that people lacked language, thought, or cultural expression before a new script. Rather, writing operated within institutions, education systems, and conventions that placed certain demands on readers and writers. The relationship between spoken Korean and high-status written culture shaped administration, learning, and who could participate in particular forms of textual exchange.

A new script could therefore be more than a technical innovation. It could make language itself the subject of careful analysis and open additional possibilities for documenting speech. But such possibilities depended on political sponsorship, social reception, teaching, and the availability of texts.
